provenance.authoring_note: These corrected lesson notes expand outline-only or skeletal Primary 4 rows using the supplied archive's topic sequence and source documents. They are newly authored teaching explanations, not verbatim transcriptions.
provenance.delivery_policy: Do not expose corrections to students until owner approval is explicit.

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: CHANGES IN NATURE
objectives: Explain the meaning of change.
Distinguish temporary changes from permanent changes.
Give examples of both types of change.
corrections.lesson: A change happens when something becomes different from its earlier form, condition or position. A temporary change can be reversed: water can freeze into ice and melt back into water. A permanent change cannot easily be reversed to its original state: wood burned into ash cannot become the same piece of wood again. Changes happen in living things and non-living things. A child grows into an adult; iron may rust; and a green leaf may turn yellow. Observe changes carefully and describe what happened before and after.
examples: Ice melting into water is temporary.
A seed growing into a plant is a living change.
Burning wood into ash is permanent.
corrections.activity: Sort picture cards into temporary and permanent changes. Explain why each example belongs in its group.
evaluation: What is a change?
State two differences between temporary and permanent changes.
Give two examples of each type.

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: CHANGES IN PLANT
objectives: Identify changes that occur as a plant grows.
Describe the stages from seed to mature plant.
State conditions plants need to grow.
corrections.lesson: Plants change as they grow. A seed can absorb water and begin to germinate. A small root grows down into the soil while a shoot grows upwards. The shoot develops a stem and leaves. As the plant becomes bigger, it may produce flowers and fruits containing seeds. Plants need water, air, suitable warmth, light and nutrients from the soil to grow well. Some changes, such as a leaf opening, happen quickly; growth takes place over a longer time. Observe a plant over several days and record what changes.
examples: A bean seed can germinate into a seedling.
A young mango plant grows into a tree.
A flowering plant may later produce fruit.
corrections.activity: Place pictures of seed, seedling, young plant and mature plant in the correct order. Keep a simple plant-growth observation chart.
evaluation: Name four stages in plant growth.
List four things plants need to grow.
Why should a growing plant be watered?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: CHANGES IN ANIMALS
objectives: Describe how animals change as they grow.
Identify examples of young and adult animals.
Explain that some animals change their body form during growth.
corrections.lesson: Animals grow and change during their lives. A young animal is usually smaller than an adult and may look different from it. A puppy grows into a dog, and a kitten grows into a cat. Some animals pass through stages that look very different. A butterfly begins as an egg, becomes a caterpillar, changes into a pupa and later emerges as an adult butterfly. This process is called metamorphosis. Animals need food, water, air and a suitable place to live as they grow.
examples: A chick grows into a hen or cock.
A tadpole develops into a frog.
A caterpillar changes into a butterfly.
corrections.activity: Arrange picture cards showing the life cycles of a butterfly and a frog. Describe each stage orally.
evaluation: What is growth?
Name the stages in a butterfly's life cycle.
Give two examples of animals and their young.

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: CHANGES IN NON-LIVING THINGS
objectives: Identify changes in non-living things.
Distinguish reversible and irreversible changes.
Describe safe examples of changes caused by heating, cooling or weather.
corrections.lesson: Non-living things can change in shape, size, temperature or condition. Some changes are temporary. Water freezes into ice when cooled and melts when warmed. Other changes are permanent. Paper torn into pieces cannot return to its original sheet, and wood burned into ash cannot become the same wood again. Metals may rust when exposed to moisture and air. Changes can happen naturally or because people do something to an object. Never use fire, hot liquids or chemicals to demonstrate a change without a teacher or adult.
examples: Ice melting is reversible.
Paper tearing is not easily reversible.
Iron rusting is a change in the metal.
corrections.activity: Observe safe classroom objects and describe one change that could happen to each. Classify examples as reversible or irreversible.
evaluation: Give three examples of changes in non-living things.
What happens when ice is warmed?
Why should pupils not experiment with fire alone?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: OUR WEATHER
objectives: Explain the meaning of weather.
Identify common elements of weather.
Describe how weather affects daily activities.
corrections.lesson: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. It can change from one day to another. We describe weather by observing sunshine, rainfall, wind, cloud cover and temperature. A sunny day may be hot and bright. A rainy day has falling water from clouds. Wind is moving air, and clouds may cover part or all of the sky. Weather affects the clothes we wear, the work farmers do and the activities we can enjoy outdoors. We can observe weather without looking directly at the sun.
examples: People may use umbrellas when it rains.
Farmers may delay drying crops when the sky is cloudy.
A windy day can move leaves and branches.
corrections.activity: Observe the sky from a safe place and record whether it is sunny, cloudy, rainy or windy.
evaluation: What is weather?
Name four elements of weather.
How can rainy weather affect a school day?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: WEATHER SYMBOLS AND RECORD CHART
objectives: Recognise simple weather symbols.
Use symbols to record daily weather.
Read information from a simple weather chart.
corrections.lesson: Weather symbols are simple pictures used to show weather conditions. A sun symbol can represent sunny weather, a cloud can represent cloudy weather, and a cloud with raindrops can represent rain. A weather record chart helps us keep information for several days. Each day, observe the sky and place the correct symbol in the chart. At the end of the week, count how many days were sunny, rainy or cloudy. A chart makes it easier to compare weather from one day to another.
examples: ☀ represents sunny weather.
☁ represents cloudy weather.
A cloud with raindrops represents rainy weather.
corrections.activity: Create a five-day weather chart using symbols. Count and compare the number of sunny and rainy days.
evaluation: What is a weather symbol?
Draw or describe two weather symbols.
How does a weather chart help us?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: COLOURS
objectives: Identify primary and secondary colours.
Name colours seen in the environment.
Describe how secondary colours can be made by mixing primary colours.
corrections.lesson: Colour is what we see when light reaches our eyes from an object. Common colours include red, yellow, blue, green, orange, purple, black and white. In basic colour mixing, red, yellow and blue are called primary colours. They can be mixed in pairs to make secondary colours. Red mixed with yellow makes orange; yellow mixed with blue makes green; and blue mixed with red makes purple. A rainbow contains several colours. Use only safe paints or colouring materials and keep them away from the eyes and mouth.
examples: Red + yellow = orange.
Yellow + blue = green.
Blue + red = purple.
corrections.activity: Use three primary-colour paints to make a colour-mixing chart. Label each new colour.
evaluation: Name the three primary colours.
How can you make green?
Mention four colours you can see in the classroom.

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: MEASUREMENT
objectives: Explain measurement as finding the size or amount of something.
Identify suitable tools for measuring length and width.
Use standard units when recording measurements.
corrections.lesson: Measurement is the process of finding the size, length, width, height or amount of an object. We measure so that we can compare objects and describe them accurately. A ruler or metre rule can measure length. A tape measure can measure longer or curved distances. The centimetre is useful for small objects, while the metre is useful for longer distances. Place the zero mark of a ruler at the beginning of the object and read the number at the other end. Do not guess when a measuring tool is available.
examples: A pencil may be about 15 centimetres long.
A classroom door may be about 2 metres high.
A tape measure can measure a desk.
corrections.activity: Measure three safe classroom objects with a ruler or tape measure and record the results with units.
evaluation: What is measurement?
Name two tools used to measure length.
Why must we write the unit beside a measurement?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: MEASURING LIQUIDS
objectives: Identify tools used to measure liquids.
Read simple liquid measurements in millilitres and litres.
Compare the capacities of different containers.
corrections.lesson: Capacity tells us how much liquid a container can hold. We measure small quantities in millilitres (mL) and larger quantities in litres (L). One litre is equal to one thousand millilitres. A measuring jug or graduated cylinder has markings that help us read the amount of liquid. Place the container on a flat surface and read the level carefully. For clear water, look at the bottom of the curved surface of the water at eye level. Never taste liquids used in a science activity.
examples: A small medicine cup may hold a few millilitres.
A bottle may hold 500 mL.
A large water container may hold 5 L.
corrections.activity: Compare the capacities printed on clean, empty bottles. Arrange them from smallest to largest.
evaluation: What is capacity?
How many millilitres make one litre?
Name one tool used to measure liquids.

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: MEASURING SOLIDS
objectives: Distinguish regular solids from irregular solids.
Measure the dimensions of a regular solid.
Describe how water displacement can help estimate the volume of an irregular solid under teacher supervision.
corrections.lesson: Solids have shapes and occupy space. A regular solid has a shape that can be described using familiar measurements, such as a cube or cuboid. We can measure its length, width and height with a ruler. An irregular solid has an uneven shape, such as a small stone. Its volume can be estimated by observing how much the water level rises when it is placed in a measuring container by a teacher. Never put unknown, sharp or dirty objects into water used for drinking.
examples: A dice is approximately cube-shaped.
A rectangular box is a cuboid.
A small clean stone is irregular in shape.
corrections.activity: Sort safe classroom objects into regular and irregular solids. Measure the length, width and height of a small box.
evaluation: What is a regular solid?
Give two examples of irregular solids.
Which tool can measure the sides of a box?

corrections.subject: Basic Science
corrections.title: MEASURING TIME
objectives: Identify common units of time.
Read time to the hour and half-hour on an analogue clock.
Use a calendar to identify days and months.
corrections.lesson: Time tells us when an event happens and how long it lasts. We measure time in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. There are 60 seconds in one minute and 60 minutes in one hour. A clock has a short hand that shows hours and a long hand that shows minutes. A calendar helps us find dates, days and months. We use time to organise school lessons, meals, rest and other daily activities. Practise reading a clock and checking the time of familiar events.
examples: A school lesson may last 40 minutes.
There are 24 hours in one day.
A week has seven days.
corrections.activity: Use a classroom clock to show 3 o'clock and half past 6. Find today's date on a calendar.
evaluation: How many minutes are in one hour?
What does the short hand show?
How many days are in one week?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: MEANING AND DEFINITION OF ARTS
objectives: Explain art in simple terms.
Identify examples of visual and performing arts.
State ways art is useful in everyday life.
corrections.lesson: Art is a creative way people express ideas, feelings and experiences. People make art by drawing, painting, modelling, weaving, singing, dancing and acting. Visual arts are works we can see, such as paintings, drawings, sculptures and designs. Performing arts are presented through actions, sound or movement, such as music, drama and dance. Art can beautify homes and public places, communicate messages, preserve culture and help people remember important events. Artists use imagination, observation and practice to improve their work.
examples: A drawing is a visual artwork.
A song is a performing art.
A poster can communicate a public message.
corrections.activity: Look at pictures of artworks and group them as visual or performing arts. Explain one use of each.
evaluation: What is art?
Name two visual arts and two performing arts.
Give three ways art is useful.

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: ELEMENTS AND PRINCIPLES OF ARTS AND DESIGN
objectives: Identify common elements of art and design.
Explain simple design principles.
Use elements and principles to arrange a clear design.
corrections.lesson: Elements of art are the basic parts artists use to make an artwork. They include line, shape, colour, texture, form and space. Principles of design describe how these elements are arranged. Examples include balance, contrast, pattern, rhythm, emphasis and unity. A design can look balanced when its parts are arranged so that one side does not appear too heavy. Contrast helps different parts stand out. Repetition can create a pattern. Artists choose and arrange elements to make their work clear, interesting and attractive.
examples: Lines can form the outline of a house.
Different colours can create contrast.
Repeated shapes can form a pattern.
corrections.activity: Design a simple greeting card using at least three elements and two design principles. Label them.
evaluation: Name four elements of art.
What is balance in a design?
How can repetition create a pattern?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: LINES
objectives: Define a line in art.
Identify different types of lines.
Use lines to create simple patterns and pictures.
corrections.lesson: A line is a mark made when a point moves across a surface. Lines can be straight, curved, horizontal, vertical, diagonal, wavy, zigzag or spiral. Artists use lines to show edges, movement, direction and texture. A horizontal line goes from side to side, while a vertical line goes up and down. A diagonal line slants. Curved and wavy lines bend. Different lines can be combined to make patterns, borders, objects and pictures. Draw lines carefully and keep them within the space provided.
examples: A standing tree trunk may be shown with vertical lines.
A calm sea may be shown with horizontal lines.
A zigzag line can show lightning.
corrections.activity: Fill a page with labelled examples of six different line types. Use them to decorate a border.
evaluation: What is a line?
Name five types of lines.
Which line type can show a slanting direction?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: SHAPES
objectives: Explain the meaning of shape.
Identify common geometric and free-form shapes.
Combine shapes to make a simple design.
corrections.lesson: A shape is a flat enclosed area with an outline. Geometric shapes have regular forms, such as circles, squares, rectangles and triangles. Free-form shapes have irregular outlines and may be found in nature. Shapes can be used to make pictures, patterns, signs and decorations. We can combine simple shapes to draw more complex objects. For example, a house can be made with a rectangle and a triangle, while a person can be drawn using circles and other simple shapes. Colour and arrange shapes neatly.
examples: A window may be a rectangle.
A wheel is circular.
A roof may be drawn as a triangle.
corrections.activity: Draw a house, a vehicle or an animal using at least four different shapes. Label the shapes.
evaluation: What is a shape?
Name four geometric shapes.
Give one example of a free-form shape.

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: DRAWING
objectives: Explain drawing as an art activity.
Identify common drawing materials.
Use lines and shapes to draw an observed object.
corrections.lesson: Drawing is making pictures or designs with lines, shapes and marks on a surface. Artists draw to record what they see, imagine new things or communicate ideas. Drawing materials include pencils, crayons, coloured pencils, charcoal, paper, erasers and sharpeners. A drawing may be realistic, imaginative or abstract. When drawing an object, look carefully at its overall shape, size and important parts. Begin with light outlines, add details and shade areas to show light and dark. Keep materials clean and use sharpeners safely.
examples: A pencil can draw the outline of a cup.
Crayons can add colour.
Shading can make a ball look round.
corrections.activity: Observe a cup or fruit and draw its outline. Add details and light shading.
evaluation: What is drawing?
Name four drawing materials.
Why should an artist observe an object carefully?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: COLOURS
objectives: Identify primary and secondary colours.
Explain how secondary colours are made.
Use colour to improve an artwork.
corrections.lesson: Colour makes an artwork attractive and can help communicate feelings or ideas. In basic colour mixing, red, yellow and blue are primary colours. Mixing two primary colours in suitable amounts makes a secondary colour: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, and blue and red make purple. Light and dark shades can be made by changing how much colour is used or by adding white or black where suitable. Artists select colours to create contrast, harmony and emphasis. Use paints and crayons carefully.
examples: Red and yellow make orange.
Yellow and blue make green.
Blue and red make purple.
corrections.activity: Make a colour wheel showing the three primary colours and the secondary colours made from them.
evaluation: Name the primary colours.
How is orange made?
What is one reason artists use colour?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: PRINT MAKING
objectives: Explain print making.
Identify safe materials used for simple prints.
Make a repeated pattern using a simple printing method.
corrections.lesson: Print making is making pictures or patterns by transferring an image from one surface onto another. A simple print can be made with a leaf, sponge, potato shape or prepared stamp. The surface is covered lightly with washable paint and pressed onto paper. The printed shape can be repeated to form a pattern. Different leaves have different shapes and veins, so they can make interesting prints. Use only safe materials approved by the teacher. Do not taste paint, and wash hands after the activity.
examples: A leaf can print its outline and veins.
A sponge can make repeated marks.
A stamp can print the same shape many times.
corrections.activity: Use a clean leaf and washable paint to make a repeated border on paper under teacher supervision.
evaluation: What is print making?
Name three materials that can make prints.
How can repeated prints form a pattern?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: DRAWING MATERIALS AND STILL-LIFE OBJECTS
objectives: Identify materials used for drawing.
Explain still-life drawing.
Arrange and draw a group of objects.
corrections.lesson: Still-life drawing is drawing objects that are arranged and remain still while the artist observes them. The objects may be natural, such as fruit, leaves and shells, or man-made, such as cups, books and bottles. Drawing materials include paper, pencils, erasers, crayons and rulers. Place the objects where they can be seen clearly. Notice their shapes, sizes, positions and how light falls on them. Draw the largest shapes first, then add smaller details. Shading can show which parts are bright and which are in shadow.
examples: A bowl of fruit is a still-life arrangement.
A bottle and a cup can be drawn together.
A leaf is a natural object.
corrections.activity: Arrange three safe objects on a table and draw them as a still-life picture.
evaluation: What is still-life drawing?
Give two natural and two man-made objects.
Why is shading useful in drawing?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: MODELLING I: PAPER-MÂCHÉ
objectives: Explain modelling and paper-mâché.
Identify materials used to make paper-mâché.
Describe safe steps for preparing a simple paper-mâché material.
corrections.lesson: Modelling is shaping a material to make a three-dimensional object. Paper-mâché is a modelling material made from paper that has been torn or mashed and mixed with a suitable paste. The soft material can be pressed around a simple mould or shaped by hand. Materials may include clean waste paper, water, a bowl and a teacher-approved paste. Allow the material to dry fully before decorating it. Use clean paper and keep the work area tidy. Pupils should not heat mixtures or use sharp tools without adult supervision.
examples: A small bowl can be used as a mould.
Mashed paper can be shaped into a simple figure.
A dry paper-mâché object can be painted.
corrections.activity: Observe a teacher demonstration of preparing paper pulp and discuss how the material changes as it dries.
evaluation: What is modelling?
What is paper-mâché made from?
Why must a paper-mâché object dry before painting?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: MODELLING II: OBJECTS MADE FROM PAPER-MÂCHÉ
objectives: Identify objects that can be made from paper-mâché.
Describe how a simple paper-mâché object is shaped.
Explain why the finished object should be dried and decorated carefully.
corrections.lesson: Paper-mâché can be used to make light decorative objects. The paper pulp is shaped by hand or pressed over a simple mould. The maker smooths the surface and leaves the object to dry completely. When it is dry and firm, it can be decorated with safe paint or coloured paper. A finished object should be handled carefully because it may break if it is dropped or becomes wet. Reusing clean waste paper for art can reduce waste and encourage creativity.
examples: A small mask can be made from paper-mâché.
A simple bowl-shaped ornament can be formed over a mould.
A model animal can be shaped from paper pulp.
corrections.activity: Sketch an object that could be made from paper-mâché and label its parts and materials.
evaluation: Name three objects that can be made from paper-mâché.
Why must the object dry completely?
How can reusing paper help the environment?

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: INTRODUCTION TO MUSIC
objectives: Explain music.
Identify common sources of sound.
Distinguish organised musical sounds from unwanted noise.
corrections.lesson: Music is an organised arrangement of sounds that people make for enjoyment, worship, celebration, communication and cultural activities. Sounds can come from the human voice, musical instruments and objects around us. Music may have rhythm, melody and a steady beat. Noise is usually an unwanted or unpleasant sound, although the same sound may be useful in a different situation. We can sing, clap, tap or play simple instruments to make music. Listen carefully and keep sounds at a comfortable level so that they do not harm hearing.
examples: Singing is a source of music.
A drum can produce a beat.
A loud vehicle horn may be unwanted noise.
corrections.activity: Listen to short examples of singing, drumming and everyday sounds. Describe which sounds form music and why.
evaluation: What is music?
Name three sources of musical sound.
State one difference between music and noise.

corrections.subject: Cultural & Creative Arts
corrections.title: MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS AND SOUNDS
objectives: Identify local musical instruments.
Describe how selected instruments produce sound.
Group instruments by how they are played.
corrections.lesson: Musical instruments are objects made or adapted to produce sounds for music. In many Nigerian communities, instruments include drums, talking drums, shekere, bata, agogo, flutes and local string instruments. A drum produces sound when its stretched surface is struck. A shaker makes sound when its contents move. A flute produces sound when air is blown through it. Instruments may be struck, shaken, blown or plucked. Different communities use instruments during ceremonies, festivals, storytelling and other events.
examples: A drum is struck.
A shekere is shaken.
A flute is blown.
corrections.activity: Display pictures or safe examples of local instruments. Pupils group them as struck, shaken, blown or plucked.
evaluation: What is a musical instrument?
Name four instruments used in Nigeria.
How does a shaker produce sound?

corrections.subject: English Language
corrections.title: WRITING: COMPOSITION ABOUT MY FAMILY; STRUCTURE AND SPELLING
objectives: Plan and write a short composition about family.
Arrange ideas in a clear beginning, middle and ending.
Use correct spelling, capital letters and full stops.
corrections.lesson: A composition is a piece of writing about a topic. Before writing about your family, think of the people in your family and what you want to say about them. Begin with an opening sentence that introduces your family. In the middle, write a few sentences about family members, what they do and how you help one another. End with a sentence explaining why your family is important to you. Use capital letters at the beginning of sentences and for names. Put a full stop at the end of a statement. Read your work again and correct spelling mistakes.
examples: My family lives in Ibadan.
My sister helps me arrange our books.
We enjoy eating together.
corrections.activity: Make a five-point plan, then write a paragraph of six to eight sentences titled 'My Family'. Exchange work with a partner to check punctuation.
evaluation: What is a composition?
Name three parts of a short composition.
Why should you reread your writing?

corrections.subject: English Language
corrections.title: ANTONYMS
objectives: Explain the meaning of antonyms.
Identify words with opposite meanings.
Use antonyms correctly in simple sentences.
corrections.lesson: Antonyms are words that have opposite or nearly opposite meanings. Learning antonyms helps us describe people, objects and actions more clearly. Some words have one common opposite, while others may have different opposites depending on the sentence. Read each word carefully and choose an opposite that makes sense. For example, happy can mean the opposite of sad, and empty can be the opposite of full. Use the words in sentences to show that you understand their meanings.
examples: happy — sad
new — old
empty — full
bright — dull
corrections.activity: Make two columns headed WORD and ANTONYM. Match word cards, then write three pairs in sentences.
evaluation: What is an antonym?
Give antonyms for awake, weak and slow.
Write a sentence using a pair of antonyms.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: ORDERING OF FRACTIONS
objectives: Explain how to compare simple fractions.
Find equivalent fractions with small denominators.
Arrange fractions in ascending and descending order.
corrections.lesson: A fraction shows part of a whole. The top number is the numerator and the bottom number is the denominator. When two fractions have the same denominator, compare their numerators: 2/5 is less than 4/5. Equivalent fractions have the same value, even when their numbers look different. For example, 1/2 is equal to 2/4. To compare fractions with different denominators, use pictures or find equivalent fractions with a common denominator. Ascending order means smallest to largest; descending order means largest to smallest.
corrections.activity: Use fraction strips or paper folded into equal parts to compare and order four fractions.
evaluation: What is a numerator?
Write a fraction equivalent to 1/2.
Arrange 1/4, 3/4 and 2/4 in ascending order.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: PROPER, IMPROPER AND MIXED FRACTIONS
objectives: Identify proper and improper fractions.
Change an improper fraction to a mixed number.
Represent fractions using drawings.
corrections.lesson: A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator, such as 3/5. An improper fraction has a numerator equal to or greater than its denominator, such as 7/4. A mixed number contains a whole number and a proper fraction, such as 1 3/4. To change 7/4 to a mixed number, divide 7 by 4. The quotient is 1 and the remainder is 3, so 7/4 = 1 3/4. Draw equal parts to help you understand why the conversion works.
examples: 2/5 is a proper fraction.
9/4 is an improper fraction.
corrections.activity: Draw shapes divided into equal parts to show one proper fraction and one improper fraction. Convert 5/2 and 11/3.
evaluation: What is a proper fraction?
Give one example of an improper fraction.
Change 7/3 to a mixed number.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: DECIMAL FRACTIONS
objectives: Read and write simple decimal fractions.
Explain tenths and hundredths using place value.
Compare and order simple decimals.
corrections.lesson: A decimal fraction is a number written with a decimal point. The first digit after the decimal point shows tenths, and the second digit shows hundredths. For example, 0.4 means four tenths, while 0.25 means twenty-five hundredths. A zero can be important when it shows place value: 0.5 is the same as 0.50, but 0.05 is smaller. To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare digits from left to right. Money and measurements often use decimals.
examples: 0.3 means three tenths.
0.25 means twenty-five hundredths.
0.7 is greater than 0.4.
corrections.activity: Use a place-value chart to write and compare decimal numbers. Place simple decimal amounts on a number line.
evaluation: What does the first digit after the decimal point represent?
Which is greater: 0.6 or 0.4?
Write five tenths as a decimal.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: ADDITION OF WHOLE NUMBERS
objectives: Add whole numbers accurately.
Use place value to add numbers with several digits.
Solve simple word problems involving addition.
corrections.lesson: Addition combines two or more numbers to find a total. Write numbers in columns so that units are under units, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds and so on. Add from the units column, regrouping when a column totals ten or more. For example, 2,468 + 1,357 = 3,825. Check your answer by adding in a different order or estimating first. Addition is useful when finding totals, counting items and working out how many objects there are altogether.
corrections.activity: Work in pairs to solve three addition problems and one word problem about items sold in a shop.
evaluation: What does addition find?
Why should digits be placed in the correct columns?
Calculate 3,475 + 2,368.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: SUBTRACTION OF WHOLE NUMBERS
objectives: Subtract whole numbers using place value.
Regroup when a digit in the top number is too small.
Solve word problems involving difference and remainder.
corrections.lesson: Subtraction means taking one number away from another or finding the difference between two numbers. Arrange the numbers in columns, keeping units, tens, hundreds and thousands in the correct places. Subtract from the units column. If the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit, regroup from the next column. For example, 5,204 − 1,786 = 3,418. Estimate before calculating and check by adding the answer to the number taken away. The result should equal the starting number.
corrections.activity: Use place-value counters or drawings to demonstrate regrouping. Solve a word problem about money remaining after a purchase.
evaluation: What does subtraction find?
What is regrouping?
Calculate 6,000 − 2,745.

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: ADDITION AND SUBTRACTION OF FRACTIONS
objectives: Add fractions with the same denominator.
Subtract fractions with the same denominator.
Solve simple fraction word problems.
corrections.lesson: When fractions have the same denominator, the parts are the same size. To add them, add the numerators and keep the denominator. For example, 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. To subtract, subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 6/8 − 2/8 = 4/8. Simplify a fraction when the numerator and denominator can be divided by the same number. When denominators are different, first find equivalent fractions with a common denominator. Use drawings to check that the answer is sensible.
corrections.activity: Use fraction strips to model addition and subtraction. Write a matching number sentence for each drawing.
evaluation: Calculate 3/9 + 4/9.
Calculate 7/10 − 3/10.
Why must the parts be the same size before adding fractions?

corrections.subject: Mathematics
corrections.title: ADDITION AND SUBTRACTION OF DECIMAL NUMBERS
objectives: Add decimal numbers with matching place values.
Subtract decimal numbers accurately.
Solve simple money and measurement problems using decimals.
corrections.lesson: To add or subtract decimal numbers, line up the decimal points so that tenths are under tenths and hundredths are under hundredths. Add zeros at the end when needed to make the place values clear. For example, 2.35 + 1.20 = 3.55. For subtraction, 5.00 − 2.75 = 2.25. Keep the decimal point in the answer directly below the other decimal points. Check your answer by estimating or using the inverse operation. Decimals are useful when working with money and measurements.
corrections.activity: Use pretend shop prices to add two costs and calculate change. Show each calculation with aligned decimal points.
evaluation: Why do we line up decimal points?
Calculate 3.40 + 2.35.
Calculate 8.00 − 3.65.
